facts: The Selfridges building at the Bullring, completed in 2003, is covered in over 15,000 aluminium discs.
Birmingham New Street is one of the busiest interchange stations in the UK outside London.
The Bullring has been a market site in Birmingham for over 800 years.
The Jewellery Quarter still produces around 40% of all jewellery made in the UK.
It holds the highest concentration of jewellery businesses in Europe.
The Museum of the Jewellery Quarter preserves a former working jewellery factory exactly as it was left.
Bournville was built as a model village by the Cadbury family to house their chocolate factory workers from 1893.
The factory remains one of the largest chocolate producers in Europe.
Bournville was designed with generous green space, strongly influencing the later garden city movement.
Coventry's medieval cathedral was destroyed in a single night of bombing in November 1940.
A new modernist cathedral was built alongside the ruins, consecrated in 1962.
Coventry is linked to the legend of Lady Godiva, said to have ridden naked through the streets in protest at taxation.
Warwick Castle began as a wooden fort built by William the Conqueror in 1068.
It is now one of the most visited castles in Britain, run as a major visitor attraction.
Warwick's medieval town centre survived a great fire in 1694 that destroyed much of the rest of the town.
William Shakespeare was born and grew up in this half-timbered house on Henley Street in 1564.
The Royal Shakespeare Theatre, on the riverbank, remains one of Britain's leading theatre companies.
Stratford-upon-Avon attracts millions of visitors from around the world each year.
Kenilworth Castle was besieged for six months in 1266, one of the longest sieges in English history.
Elizabeth I visited multiple times, hosted by Robert Dudley in lavish entertainments.
The castle's ruins are among the largest of any in England.
Leamington Spa grew rapidly as a fashionable spa town after Queen Victoria granted it 'Royal' status in 1838.
Its Pump Rooms, built in 1814, once offered visitors mineral water treatments.
The town has some of the finest Regency architecture outside London and Bath.
Worcester Cathedral holds the tomb of King John, who requested burial there in 1216.
The cathedral overlooks the Three Choirs Festival, one of the world's oldest music festivals.
Worcester is famous for Worcestershire sauce and Royal Worcester porcelain.
Composer Edward Elgar lived much of his life near the Malvern Hills and drew inspiration from them.
Malvern developed as a Victorian 'water cure' spa town, exploiting its pure hill springs.
Great Malvern Priory has some of the finest surviving medieval stained glass in England.
The Severn Valley Railway is one of the longest standard-gauge heritage railways in Britain, running to Bridgnorth.
Kidderminster was historically the centre of the British carpet-weaving industry.
The town's Museum of Carpet preserves this heritage in a former Victorian factory.
Wembley Stadium's arch, at 133 metres, is the longest single-span roof structure in the world.
It is the home of the England national football team.
The original Wembley Stadium, with its twin towers, hosted the 1966 World Cup Final.
High Wycombe was once the centre of British chair-making, nicknamed 'Chairborough' locally.
The town's Wycombe Museum tells the story of its furniture trade.
High Wycombe sits in the Chiltern Hills, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Bicester Village is one of the most visited outlet shopping destinations in Europe.
It has its own dedicated railway station, opened in 2015 to serve the growing site.
Bicester itself has Roman origins, with the remains of a fort nearby.
The Bodleian Library is one of the oldest libraries in Europe, dating from 1602.
Oxford is home to the oldest university in the English-speaking world.
Oxford station sits a short walk from the city's historic colleges.
Blenheim Palace was the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill in 1874.
It is the only non-royal, non-episcopal country house in England to hold the title 'palace'.
Oxford Parkway is a park-and-ride station opened in 2015 on the edge of the city.
The nursery rhyme 'Ride a Cock Horse to Banbury Cross' refers to this Oxfordshire market town.
Banbury has been famous for Banbury cakes, a spiced pastry, since at least the 17th century.
The current Banbury Cross monument was erected in 1859 to mark Princess Victoria's wedding.
Amersham has two distinct centres: the historic Old Town and the newer area around the station, built during Metro-land expansion.
The town was heavily promoted by the Metropolitan Railway in the early 20th century as an idyllic commuter suburb.
Amersham's Old Town retains 16th and 17th century coaching inns.
Chorleywood Common is one of the largest expanses of common land close to London.
The village grew rapidly as 'Metro-land' commuter housing from the 1900s onward.
Chorleywood was named the best place to live in Britain by a Channel 4 survey in 2011.
The station serves both Chalfont St Giles, where Milton completed Paradise Lost, and the village of Latimer.
The surrounding Chess Valley is a designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Chalfont & Latimer is a junction for the branch line to Chesham.
Roald Dahl lived near Aylesbury for much of his life, and the Roald Dahl Museum is in nearby Great Missenden.
Aylesbury is the county town of Buckinghamshire.
The town gave its name to the Aylesbury duck breed, once farmed extensively in the area.
Roald Dahl lived in Great Missenden for 36 years, writing many of his best-known children's books there.
The Roald Dahl Museum and Story Centre occupies buildings in the village centre.
Great Missenden sits in the Chiltern Hills, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Bekonscot is the oldest original model village in the world, opened in 1929.
Beaconsfield has both an Old Town and a newer town, similar to Amersham's dual layout.
The village model railway at Bekonscot has run continuously since it opened.

landmark: Gerrards Cross & the Chiltern commuter belt
facts: Gerrards Cross has long been one of the most affluent commuter towns on the Chiltern Main Line.
The village sits within the Metropolitan Green Belt around London.
Its station has served London commuters since the Great Western and Great Central Joint Railway opened in 1906.
Harrow School, founded in 1572, has educated seven British prime ministers including Winston Churchill.
The hilltop town offers views across much of northwest London.
Harrow-on-the-Hill is a major interchange between the Chiltern line and London Underground.
Molineux has been the home of Wolverhampton Wanderers since 1889.
Wolverhampton was historically a major centre of lock, key and japanned metalware manufacturing.
The city's name derives from Wulfrun, an Anglo-Saxon noblewoman who founded a monastery there.
Lichfield Cathedral is the only medieval English cathedral with three spires.
Dr Samuel Johnson, compiler of an influential early English dictionary, was born in Lichfield in 1709.
The cathedral holds the 8th-century St Chad Gospels, an important illuminated manuscript.
Stafford Castle's Norman motte is one of the largest in England.
The town is the county town of Staffordshire.
Stafford was historically a centre of shoemaking, particularly for the boot and shoe trade.

landmark: Rugby School & the birthplace of rugby football
facts: Rugby football takes its name from Rugby School, where the game is said to have originated in 1823.
A plaque at the school commemorates William Webb Ellis, credited with first picking up the ball and running with it.
Rugby is a major railway junction town in Warwickshire.
Novelist George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) was born near Nuneaton in 1819.
The town was historically a centre of textile weaving and coal mining.
Nuneaton sits in northern Warwickshire, close to the Leicestershire border.
Solihull is one of the most affluent towns in the West Midlands.
The nearby Jaguar Land Rover plant is one of the region's largest employers.
Solihull's medieval church, St Alphege, dominates the town's historic core.
Redditch was once the world's leading centre for needle manufacturing.
The Forge Mill Needle Museum preserves one of the last working needle mills.
Redditch was designated a post-war new town in 1964.
Droitwich's brine springs are around ten times saltier than the Dead Sea.
The town was a major Victorian spa resort, promoted for its therapeutic salt baths.
Droitwich has been a centre of salt production since Roman times.
Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings rescues and rebuilds threatened timber-framed buildings on one site.
Bromsgrove was historically known for nail-making and, later, the Austin Motor Company's nearby Longbridge plant.
Bromsgrove sits in the Worcestershire countryside south of Birmingham.
Longbridge was home to one of Britain's largest car factories, founded by Herbert Austin in 1905.
At its peak, the plant employed tens of thousands of workers producing Austin and later MG Rover cars.
Part of the former factory site has been redeveloped as a technology and business park.
Sutton Park is one of the largest urban parks in Europe, covering over 2,400 acres.
The park retains ancient woodland, heathland and wetland habitats within a city boundary.
Sutton Coldfield received a royal charter from Henry VIII in 1528.
Villa Park has been Aston Villa's home ground since 1897.
It has hosted more FA Cup semi-finals than any other stadium.
Aston is one of Birmingham's oldest inner suburbs, with a manor house dating to the 1630s.
Dudley Castle's ruins now house a zoo within the medieval fortress grounds.
Dudley sits at the heart of the Black Country, named for the heavy industry and coal that once blackened the landscape.
The town has no mainline station of its own; Dudley Port is the nearest stop.
The Black Country Living Museum recreates a 19th and early 20th century industrial town, with costumed guides.
Tipton sits at the centre of the historic Black Country industrial region.
The area was named for the soot and smoke that once blackened its skies and soil.
Stourbridge was once the centre of English glassmaking, producing fine crystal for centuries.
The Red House Glass Cone, a rare surviving 19th-century glass cone kiln, still stands in the town.
Stourbridge Town station is served by a short branch line, one of Britain's shortest scheduled rail journeys.
Walsall was historically the centre of the British saddlery and leather goods industry.
The Walsall Leather Museum occupies a former Victorian leather factory.
Walsall sits at the northern edge of the Black Country.
Wootton Wawen's parish church has an Anglo-Saxon tower, among the oldest structures of its kind in Warwickshire.
The Stratford-upon-Avon Canal passes directly through the village on a tall aqueduct.
Wootton Wawen sits in the Forest of Arden countryside.
Henley-in-Arden's mile-long High Street retains an almost unbroken run of historic buildings.
The town sits within the historic Forest of Arden, an area associated with Shakespeare's plays.
Henley-in-Arden received its market charter in the 13th century.
Ledbury's Market House, built around 1617, stands on 16 wooden pillars in the town centre.
The town's cobbled Church Lane is one of the most photographed streets in Herefordshire.
Ledbury was the birthplace of poet John Masefield.

landmark: Colwall & the Malvern Hills' western slopes
facts: Colwall sits on the western, Herefordshire side of the Malvern Hills.
The village has long been associated with spring water bottling.
Colwall Tunnel, on the line to Ledbury, was for many years the longest tunnel on a British branch line.
Telford was designated a new town in 1968, named after engineer Thomas Telford.
It absorbed several older industrial towns including Ironbridge, birthplace of the Industrial Revolution.
Telford Central station serves the town's modern shopping and business district.
Ironbridge Gorge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, home to the world's first iron bridge, built in 1779.
The RAF Museum Midlands, at Cosford, displays historic military aircraft.
Cosford station is the nearest railhead to both attractions.
The Wedgwood Museum, near Barlaston, tells the story of Josiah Wedgwood's pioneering pottery firm.
Wedgwood moved production to Barlaston in the 1940s, building a model factory village.
Barlaston sits in the Staffordshire Potteries region.
The Hawthorns has been West Bromwich Albion's home ground since 1900.
It is the highest-altitude ground in English top-flight football history.
The station serves both the stadium and the boundary between Birmingham and Sandwell.
Alexander Stadium was the main venue for the 2022 Commonwealth Games, hosted in Birmingham.
The stadium underwent a major redevelopment ahead of the games.
Perry Barr sits in north Birmingham, on the line towards Walsall.
